question: Tell me about a time you noticed an issue in someone's work that could have blown up at a design review. How did you raise it early and in private?

raiseTranscript.text: I was reviewing a teammate's PR for a new API endpoint and spotted that error handling was missing for a rate-limit case. It could have caused a 500 at the design review demo. I messaged them privately on Slack with the exact line and a suggested test case.
They thanked me, added the test, and we shipped clean. Later they asked me to review another change.
How did you decide to go private instead of commenting on the PR?
I figured a public comment might feel like showing them up in front of the team, so I kept it between us.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you noticed an issue in someone's work that could have blown up at a design review. How did you raise it early and in private?
Role: new grad on small team, spotted missing rate-limit handling in peer PR
Action: sent private Slack note with line number and test suggestion instead of PR comment
Outcome: fixed before review; peer later asked for more reviews
Quote: "I figured a public comment might feel like showing them up"
Follow-up: How did you decide private vs public? Candidate explained intent to protect teammate's reputation
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Earn Trust for this question. Junior candidate described noticing a missing rate-limit case in a peer's PR that risked a 500 at review. They chose a private Slack note with the exact line and a test suggestion rather than a public comment. The change was made before the review and the peer later requested more input from them. This shows early ownership of their own review work plus awareness of how public feedback lands. Biggest strength is the deliberate choice to protect the teammate's standing while still driving the fix.

lowerTranscript.text: I saw a teammate's design had a missing auth check that would have failed at review. I left a comment on the doc and also mentioned it in the team channel so everyone could see.
I wanted to make sure it got fixed and didn't want to risk it being missed.

raiseTranscript.text: While reviewing cross-team API specs I found an inconsistency in how retries were defined that would surface as a latency spike in the design review. I scheduled a 15-minute 1:1 with the owning engineer and walked through the numbers.
They updated the spec, the review went smoothly, and the two teams later adopted a shared retry library I suggested.
How did you frame the conversation?
I started by saying I had seen the same pattern cause issues on my prior team and wanted to save them the same pain.

Did you talk to the engineer first?
No, I wanted to make sure it was addressed quickly through the right chain.

This shows the candidate defaulted to hierarchy instead of building trust through direct, private conversation. Biggest gap is missing the step of attempting a low-authority, peer-level discussion first.

raiseTranscript.text: During a quarterly planning review I noticed two product teams had conflicting assumptions on data retention that would have created a compliance risk at the architecture review. I pulled the two GMs into a private meeting before the larger forum.
We agreed on a 90-day retention policy with a clear exception process; both teams accepted the short-term scope cut to avoid a later audit finding.
How did you keep it from becoming political?
I framed it as protecting the company's regulatory standing rather than picking a winner between the teams.

I thought the broader group needed to see the disagreement to make the right call.
